facts.statement: Magnapaulia was a herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous in Baja California, northwestern Mexico.
facts.quote: Magnapaulia is a genus of herbivorous lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) El Gallo Formation of Baja California, northwestern Mexico.

facts.statement: The species was first described in 1981 by William J. Morris as Lambeosaurus laticaudus based on a partial skeleton and skull.
facts.quote: Morris named them Lambeosaurus laticaudus in 1981, based on type specimen LACM 17715, a partial skeleton with partial skull.

facts.statement: The specific name laticaudus means "broad tail" in Latin.
facts.quote: The specific name is derived from the Latin latus, "broad", and cauda, "tail".

facts.statement: The original describer suggested the animal was semi-aquatic, citing a tall narrow tail, weak hips, and a healed broken thigh bone as evidence.
facts.quote: Morris interpreted this species as water-bound, due to features like its size, its tall and narrow tail (interpreted as a swimming adaptation), and weak hip articulations, as well as a healed broken thigh bone that he thought would have been too much of a handicap for a terrestrial animal to have survived long enough to heal.

facts.statement: The genus was elevated to a separate genus in 2012 by Prieto-Márquez, Chiappe, and Joshi.
facts.quote: In 2012 it was named as a separate genus by Albert Prieto-Márquez, Luis Chiappe, and Shantanu Joshi.

facts.statement: The genus name honors Paul G. Haaga Jr., combining the Latin word for large with his first name.
facts.quote: The generic name is a combination of the Latin magnus, "large", and the first name of Paul G. Haaga Jr., the president of the board of trustees of the Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: Fossils date to the late Campanian stage, approximately 73.6 to 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: The 2012 study indicated that the remains had been found in a layer of the El Gallo Formation, dating to the late Campanian, about 73.6 to 73 million years old.

facts.statement: The original describer estimated the animal reached lengths of 15 to 16.5 meters and weighed up to 8 metric tons.
facts.quote: Its size was estimated by its original describer as between 15 m (49.2 ft) and 16.5 m (54.1 ft) long, with a body mass of up to 8 metric tons (8.8 tons).

facts.statement: A 2012 study estimated the length at around 12.5 meters, identifying it as the largest known lambeosaurine based on a specimen with an 80.3 cm humerus.
facts.quote: Prieto-Márquez et al. (2012) provided a smaller estimate of around 12.5 m, still among the longest ornithischians and representing the largest known lambeosaurine, based on the largest known specimen (LACM 17712) with a humerus estimated at 80.3 cm in length.

facts.statement: Estimates suggest the animal could have weighed up to 9.77 metric tons.
facts.quote: It has been estimated that Magnapaulia would have weighed up to 9.77 MT.

facts.statement: Unique features include tail chevrons four times longer than vertebrae and front joint processes at the tail base forming a deep trough.
facts.quote: The redescription of 2012 established two autapomorphies, unique derived traits: the presence of chevrons at the tail base that were four times as long as the vertebral centra; and the possession at the tail base vertebrae of front joint processes, prezygapophyses, the inner bases of which formed a bowl-shaped depression that extended upwards into a deep trough on the front surface of the spine.

facts.statement: A tall crest of spines ran from the middle of the back to the middle of the tail, with spines four times higher than the vertebrae.
facts.quote: On the vertebral column, from at least the middle of the back to over the middle of the tail, a tall crest of almost continuous height was present formed by spines that were about four times as high as the vertebral centra.

facts.statement: Skin impressions show large scales up to four centimeters wide surrounded by smaller hexagonal and rounded scales.
facts.quote: Magnapaulia is among the many hadrosaurids that have preserved skin impressions; the tail of specimen LACM 17712 had large scales up to four centimeters wide that were surrounded by one centimeter-wide hexagonal and rounded scales.

facts.statement: Magnapaulia is classified within the subfamily Lambeosaurinae.
facts.quote: In 2012 Magnapaulia was assigned to the Lambeosaurinae.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis places Magnapaulia closest to Velafrons, forming a southern clade sister to northern Asian and North American lambeosaurines.
facts.quote: The 2012 study contained a cladistic analysis which found it to be closest to Velafrons, also from Mexico, with this sister species forming a separate southern clade, itself the sister group of a clade of more northern Asian and North-American forms, including Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, Hypacrosaurus and Olorotitan.

facts.statement: Magnapaulia laticaudus is the only known species of this extinct lambeosaurine ornithopod dinosaur.
facts.quote: Magnapaulia laticaudus es la única especie conocida del género extinto Magnapaulia de dinosaurio ornitópodo lambeosaurino que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 million years ago durante el Campaniaense en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The original describer estimated a length of 15 to 16.5 meters and a weight of over 23 tons.
facts.quote: Su tamaño fue estimado por el descriptor original entre 15 a 16,5 metros de largo, con un peso de más de 23 toneladas.

facts.statement: Between 1981 and 2012, researchers debated whether the remains belonged to Lambeosaurus, Hypacrosaurus, or represented a valid new genus.
facts.quote: Between 1981 and 2012, other authors accepted it as a potential species of Lambeosaurus, suggested it could instead be a species of Hypacrosaurus, or questioned its validity.

facts.statement: Magnapaulia fossils were found in Upper Cretaceous rocks in Baja California, northwestern Mexico.
facts.quote: Fue encontrado en rocas del Cretácico Superior en Baja California, al noroeste de México.

facts.statement: William J. Morris originally described the animal in 1981 as a possible species of Lambeosaurus named ?L. laticaudus.
facts.quote: Fue descrito originalmente en 1981 como una especie posible de Lambeosaurus (?L. laticaudus) por William J. Morris

facts.statement: Alberto Prieto-Márquez and colleagues assigned the animal to its own genus in 2012.
facts.quote: y le fue dado su propio género en 2012 por Alberto Prieto-Márquez et al.

facts.statement: Morris used a question mark for the species name because a complete crest had not been found at the time.
facts.quote: Morris usó un signo de pregunta en su trabajo porque no se había encontrado una cresta completa de esta especie

facts.statement: Morris considered the species semiaquatic, interpreting its large size and high, narrow tail as adaptations for swimming.
facts.quote: Él consideró que esta especie era semiacuática, debido a características como su tamaño, su cola alta y estrecha, interpretada como una adaptación para nadar

facts.statement: Morris thought a healed broken femur was evidence that a terrestrial animal would not have survived long enough to heal such an injury.
facts.quote: así como un fémur roto que sanó, que él pensó que era evidencia de que hubiera sido improbable que un animal terrestre sobreviviera lo suficiente como para poder sanar.

facts.statement: The generic name combines the Latin word for 'large' with the first name of Paul G. Haaga, Jr.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico es una combinación del latín magnus, "grande", y el primer nombre de Paul G. Haaga, Jr.

facts.statement: The 2012 study dated the fossils to the late Campanian stage, approximately 73.6 to 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: El estudio de 2012 indicó que los restos se habían encontrado en una capa de la Formación El Gallo, que data de finales del Campaniense., alrededor de 73,6 a 73 millones de años.

facts.statement: Magnapaulia was assigned to the subfamily Lambeosaurinae in 2012.
facts.quote: Magnapaulia fue asignado en 2012 a la subfamilia Lambeosaurinae.

facts.statement: A 2012 cladistic analysis placed Magnapaulia close to Velafrons, identifying it as the sister species.
facts.quote: El estudio de 2012 contenía un análisis cladístico que lo encontró como cercano a Velafrons, también de México, el cual constituye su especie hermana

facts.statement: The parent group of Magnapaulia is Lambeosaurini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Lambeosaurini

facts.statement: Magnapaulia belongs to the family Hadrosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Hadrosauridae

facts.statement: Magnapaulia is classified in the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: The time range for Magnapaulia is the Campanian stage, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)
